775: /** A single gatekeeper resource type in the admin resource-config UI. */
776: export type AdminResource = {
777:   /** The resource's urlPattern, used as its stable identifier. */
778:   urlPattern: string;
779:   title: string;
780:   description: string;
781:   icon?: AvatarImage;
782:   /** Whether this resource is currently enabled (not in the admin disabled set). */
783:   enabled: boolean;
784: };
785: 
786: /**
787:  * Provisioning mode for an auto-provisioning ("ambient") gatekeeper — one that mints a connected
788:  * account with no OAuth flow (VendorDescription.autoProvisionsAccount), e.g. the Context Library:
789:  *   - 'disabled': not available; no account is provisioned and any existing one is dormant.
790:  *   - 'optional': users opt in from the Connectors page; not forced on anyone (the default).
791:  *   - 'enabled':  auto-provisioned for every user (forced); they can't remove it.
792:  */
793: export const AMBIENT_GATEKEEPER_MODES = ['disabled', 'optional', 'enabled'] as const;
794: export type AmbientGatekeeperMode = typeof AMBIENT_GATEKEEPER_MODES[number];
795: 
796: export function isAmbientGatekeeperMode(value: unknown): value is AmbientGatekeeperMode {
797:   return AMBIENT_GATEKEEPER_MODES.includes(value as AmbientGatekeeperMode);
798: }
799: 
800: /**
801:  * A bound gatekeeper in the admin gatekeeper-config UI, discriminated by `autoProvisions`:
802:  *   - an ordinary OAuth/resource gatekeeper has a binary `enabled` flag and `resources` to toggle;
803:  *   - an auto-provisioning ("ambient") gatekeeper has a three-state `ambientMode` and no resources.
804:  */
805: export type AdminResourceVendor = {
806:   vendorId: string;
807:   displayName: string;
808:   logo?: AvatarImage;
809: } & (
810:   | { autoProvisions: false; enabled: boolean; resources: AdminResource[] }
811:   | { autoProvisions: true; ambientMode: AmbientGatekeeperMode }
812: );
813: 
814: /**
815:  * A connectable third-party service: its vendor id, display metadata, and the resource types it
816:  * offers (empty for an auto-provisioning gatekeeper like the Context Library). Returned by both
817:  * listGatekeeperVendors and listAddableGatekeepers so the connect UI treats both uniformly.
818:  */

820:   id: string;
821:   description: VendorDescription;
822:   supportedResources: SupportedResource[];

827:   unavailable?: boolean;
828: };

830: /** Maximum length (characters) of the admin-authored agent system-prompt instructions. */
831: export const MAX_INSTANCE_INSTRUCTIONS_LENGTH = 8000;
832: 
833: /** Maximum length (characters) of the admin-authored site name shown next to the top-bar logo. */
834: export const MAX_SITE_NAME_LENGTH = 40;
835: 
836: /**
837:  * What this deployment calls itself when the admin has not set a custom `siteName`. Also the
838:  * product's own name, so it appears in prose the server and UI address to the user.
839:  */
840: export const DEFAULT_SITE_NAME = "Cloudflare OS";
841: 
842: /**
843:  * The name to display for this deployment. Accepts an unset or not-yet-loaded `siteName` so both
844:  * the server (reading admin config) and the client (reading ServerConfig) resolve it identically.

851: export const MAX_SITE_LOGO_BYTES = 256 * 1024;

854: export const MAX_SITE_LOGO_DIMENSION = 512;

856: /** All admin-managed deployment settings, returned by AdminApi.getSettings() for the admin UI. */
857: export type AdminSettingsView = {
858:   /** Whether new account signups are allowed. */
859:   signupsEnabled: boolean;
860:   /** Site name shown next to the top-bar logo ("" falls back to DEFAULT_SITE_NAME). */
861:   siteName: string;
862:   /** Custom deployment logo, or undefined to use the default Cloudflare OS mark. */
863:   siteLogo?: AvatarImage;
864:   /** Agent system-prompt instructions ("" when unset). */

873:   resourceVendors: AdminResourceVendor[];

878: /**
879:  * One promoted blueprint, as the admin Formats panel sees it: the deployment's curation plus
880:  * enough of the blueprint to show what is being curated.
881:  */
882: export type AdminFormat = {
883:   blueprintId: string;
884: 
885:   blueprintTitle: string;
886: 
887:   /**
888:    * The blueprint's own description, which is the rest of the catalog entry the agent reads;
889:    * `agentHint` is only its last line.
890:    */
891:   blueprintDescription: string;
892: 
893:   /** Presentation after the deployment's overrides are applied. */
894:   output?: BlueprintOutput;
895: 
896:   /** What the blueprint itself declares, so the panel can show which fields are overridden. */
897:   declared?: BlueprintOutput;
898: 
899:   /** The deployment's presentation overrides, if any. */
900:   overrides?: Partial<BlueprintOutput>;
901: 
902:   enabled: boolean;
903: 
904:   /** One line telling the agent when to prefer this format. */
905:   agentHint: string;
906: 
907:   /**
908:    * The promoted blueprint no longer exists (deleted after promotion). Such an entry is skipped
909:    * everywhere else; the panel surfaces it so the admin can remove it.
910:    */

912: 
913:   /**
914:    * The blueprint ships with the deployment (see format-blueprints/ and the FORMAT_BLUEPRINTS the
915:    * build generates from it), so an upgrade can replace its contents. Curation stays the admin's: an upgrade never re-promotes something they

921: /**
922:  * Capability for managing deployment-wide admin settings, obtained via
923:  * AuthenticatedApi.getAdminApi() (which is null for non-admins). The access check happens when the
924:  * capability is minted, so these methods don't re-check. Covers branding, agent instructions, and
925:  * which gatekeeper connectors/resources are offered — NOT authentication config (that's env-var
926:  * driven). Each setter throws on invalid input.
927:  */
928: export interface AdminApi {
929:   /** Read all admin-managed settings for the admin UI in one call. */
930:   getSettings(): Promise<AdminSettingsView>;
931: 
932:   /** Enable or disable new account signups. Existing users can still log in while signups are closed. */

935:   /**

952:    * agent; it doesn't revoke a capability a gadget already holds.

954:   setResourceEnabled(vendorId: string, urlPattern: string, enabled: boolean): Promise<void>;

956:   /**

965:   /**

971:   /**

977:   /**

983:   /**

989:   /** Mark or unmark a blueprint as featured on the deployment. */

992:   // --- Standard output formats ---

1027:   enabled?: boolean;
1028:   agentHint?: string;

<content>
1: # Blueprints
2: 
3: Blueprints let a user share a gadget's source code so that others can create their own gadget instances from it. A blueprint captures the code but not the chat history, SQLite storage, or credentials. Each gadget created from a blueprint gets its own bindings, storage, and chat history.
4: 
5: This is analogous to a template: the blueprint author publishes a reusable gadget design, and anyone with the link can stamp out their own copy, pointing it at their own resources.
6: 
7: ## Key Properties
8: 
9: - A single gadget can have **multiple blueprints**, potentially at different code versions (e.g. a "stable" and a "latest" blueprint of the same gadget).
10: - Each blueprint has a **128-bit random hex ID**, generated server-side. Blueprints bundled with a deployment are the exception: they carry stable, readable IDs (see [Output Formats and Bundled Blueprints](#output-formats-and-bundled-blueprints)).
11: - Blueprints are shared via link: `https://<host>/blueprint/<blueprint-id>` (for example, a random hex ID or a bundled ID such as `format.document`).
12: - Anyone with the link can **view** the blueprint's metadata (title, description, author, required bindings) without authenticating. **Creating a gadget** from a blueprint requires authentication.
13: - A blueprint is always owned by the gadget's owner, regardless of which collaborator creates it. Bundled blueprints have no owning user at all.
14: - The blueprint author can **update** a blueprint to reflect newer code, incrementing its version number. Old code versions are retained in storage to avoid race conditions during concurrent instantiation.
15: - Blueprints can be exported to a `.gadget` file and imported into a different Workshop instance.
16: 
17: ## What a Blueprint Captures
18: 
19: A blueprint captures:
20: 
21: - **Source code** -- a snapshot of the gadget's committed Yjs document, stripped of edit history. The snapshot contains only the final file contents (one insert operation per file), producing a minimal encoding.
22: - **Binding requirements** -- a description of each named binding the gadget uses, including what type of connection is needed (gatekeeper, AI model, or agent spawner) and how to configure it. The blueprint does not include any credentials or live connections.
23: - **Metadata** -- title, description, optional screenshot metadata, author info, version number, and timestamps.
24: 
25: A blueprint does **not** capture:
26: 
27: - The gadget's SQLite storage contents.
28: - AI chat history or edit history.
29: - Live connections or credentials. Only the *shape* of each binding (its type, gatekeeper name, URL pattern, etc.) is recorded.
30: 
31: ## Binding Annotations
32: 
33: Before creating a blueprint, the author can optionally add **blueprint annotations** for the gadget's named bindings. This user-provided metadata controls how each required connection appears to someone creating a gadget from the blueprint:
34: 
35: - **Name** -- a friendly connection name shown to blueprint consumers. It defaults to the current resource title, while the binding name remains the stable key used by code.
36: - **Description** -- optional helper text that tells the blueprint consumer what kind of resource to connect.
37: - **Suggest value** -- optionally includes the specific resource URL or model name as a suggestion. This is useful when the blueprint author intends all instances to use the same resource, but it remains a suggestion rather than a requirement.
38: 
39: All named bindings are included in the blueprint. Annotations are configured in the **Blueprint** modal opened from the gadget editor header. The annotation is stored on the `GatekeeperRecord` as the `blueprintAnnotation` field.
40: 
41: ## Binding Types
42: 
43: Blueprints support three types of bindings, matching the three types of gatekeepers:
44: 
45: 1. **Gatekeeper** (`type: "gatekeeper"`) -- an external resource connection (e.g. Google Drive, a REST API). The blueprint records the gatekeeper adapter name and a URL pattern describing what kind of resource is expected. When instantiating, the user picks a connected account and configures a matching resource.
46: 
47: 2. **AI Model** (`type: "aiModel"`) -- a language model binding. The blueprint may suggest a specific provider/model. When instantiating, the user picks from their own configured models.
48: 
49: 3. **Agent Spawner** (`type: "agentSpawner"`) -- an agent spawner binding. The blueprint carries over the spawner configuration (prompt types, env restrictions) from the source gadget. The user only needs to choose which model the spawner should use (or no model).
50: 
51: ## Storage Architecture
52: 
53: Blueprint data is stored in three places, with one-way propagation: Gadget DO -> User DO -> Workers KV.
54: 
55: 1. **Gadget DO** (`blueprints` collection) -- the authoritative source. Stores `BlueprintGadgetRecord` including full metadata, the code version that was exported, and a `dirty` flag for tracking propagation failures.
56: 
57: 2. **User DO** (`blueprints` collection) -- a denormalized copy for efficient listing. Stores `BlueprintUserRecord` with metadata and a reference to the source gadget. This allows a user to audit and manage their blueprints even if the source gadget has been deleted.
58: 
59: 3. **Workers KV** (`BLUEPRINTS` namespace) -- the public-facing lookup store. Stores `BlueprintKvRecord` keyed by blueprint hex ID. This is what `PublicApi.getBlueprint()` reads from.
60: 
61: Blueprint **code content** is stored separately in an **R2 bucket** (`BLUEPRINT_CONTENT`). The R2 key is `<blueprintId>/<version>`. Content is stored as a Yjs V2-encoded document (the full state, not incremental updates). When a blueprint is updated, old versions are retained to avoid race conditions. When a blueprint is deleted, all its R2 versions are cleaned up.
62: 
63: The `dirty` flag handles propagation failures gracefully: it is set to `true` before propagation begins and cleared only after all writes succeed. If a failure leaves it set, the UI shows a warning with a "Retry" button.
64: 
65: ## Explore
66: 
67: The Explore page (`/explore`) is a place where users can discover featured blueprints. Goal is to show users what is possible and to give them place to start.
68: 
69: Admins have the ability to "feature" blueprints. This is what determines what is on this page.
70:

- Blueprints can be exported to a `.gadget` file and imported into a different Workshop instance.

## What a Blueprint Captures

A blueprint captures:

- **Source code** -- a snapshot of the gadget's committed Yjs document, stripped of edit history. The snapshot contains only the final file contents (one insert operation per file), producing a minimal encoding.
- **Binding requirements** -- a description of each named binding the gadget uses, including what type of connection is needed (gatekeeper, AI model, or agent spawner) and how to configure it. The blueprint does not include any credentials or live connections.
- **Metadata** -- title, description, optional screenshot metadata, author info, version number, and timestamps.

A blueprint does **not** capture:

- The gadget's SQLite storage contents.
- AI chat history or edit history.
- Live connections or credentials. Only the *shape* of each binding (its type, gatekeeper name, URL pattern, etc.) is recorded.

## Binding Annotations

Before creating a blueprint, the author can optionally add **blueprint annotations** for the gadget's named bindings. This user-provided metadata controls how each required connection appears to someone creating a gadget from the blueprint:

- **Name** -- a friendly connection name shown to blueprint consumers. It defaults to the current resource title, while the binding name remains the stable key used by code.
- **Description** -- optional helper text that tells the blueprint consumer what kind of resource to connect.
- **Suggest value** -- optionally includes the specific resource URL or model name as a suggestion. This is useful when the blueprint author intends all instances to use the same resource, but it remains a suggestion rather than a requirement.

All named bindings are included in the blueprint. Annotations are configured in the **Blueprint** modal opened from the gadget editor header. The annotation is stored on the `GatekeeperRecord` as the `blueprintAnnotation` field.

## Binding Types

Blueprints support three types of bindings, matching the three types of gatekeepers:

1. **Gatekeeper** (`type: "gatekeeper"`) -- an external resource connection (e.g. Google Drive, a REST API). The blueprint records the gatekeeper adapter name and a URL pattern describing what kind of resource is expected. When instantiating, the user picks a connected account and configures a matching resource.

2. **AI Model** (`type: "aiModel"`) -- a language model binding. The blueprint may suggest a specific provider/model. When instantiating, the user picks from their own configured models.

3. **Agent Spawner** (`type: "agentSpawner"`) -- an agent spawner binding. The blueprint carries over the spawner configuration (prompt types, env restrictions) from the source gadget. The user only needs to choose which model the spawner should use (or no model).

## Storage Architecture

Blueprint data is stored in three places, with one-way propagation: Gadget DO -> User DO -> Workers KV.

1. **Gadget DO** (`blueprints` collection) -- the authoritative source. Stores `BlueprintGadgetRecord` including full metadata, the code version that was exported, and a `dirty` flag for tracking propagation failures.

2. **User DO** (`blueprints` collection) -- a denormalized copy for efficient listing. Stores `BlueprintUserRecord` with metadata and a reference to the source gadget. This allows a user to audit and manage their blueprints even if the source gadget has been deleted.

3. **Workers KV** (`BLUEPRINTS` namespace) -- the public-facing lookup store. Stores `BlueprintKvRecord` keyed by blueprint hex ID. This is what `PublicApi.getBlueprint()` reads from.

Content is stored as a Yjs V2-encoded document (the full state, not incremental updates). When a blueprint is updated, old versions are retained to avoid race conditions. 40: This feature replaces that all-or-nothing posture with a per-user, gatekeeper-mediated check:
41: 
42: - **Observers.** Every non-owner who can see data the Gadget read is an *observer*. When a user
43:   becomes an observer, each relevant gatekeeper is asked — via `Gatekeeper.addObserver()` — to
44:   verify that this specific person is allowed to directly observe everything the Gadget has
45:   already read through that gatekeeper. The gatekeeper is the authority on its own resource's
46:   ACL, so the check runs inside the gatekeeper's trust domain.
47: 
48: - **Verifiers.** The overseer cannot itself reason about a vendor's identity/ACL model. Instead,
49:   the prospective observer's *own connected account* mints an opaque `GatekeeperUserVerifier`
50:   (via `GatekeeperUser.getVerifier()`), which the overseer hands back to the gatekeeper. The
51:   gatekeeper "unwraps" it (today, by calling semi-private methods it defined on its own verifier
52:   object) to learn the observer's vendor-level identity and check access.
53: 
54: - **Forward exclusion.** For observations made *after* a user becomes an observer, the gatekeeper
55:   can name observers who must not see a given observation via
56:   `ObservationDescription.excludeObservers`. The overseer must then guarantee those observers
57:   never see it, or block the observation.
58: 
59: **The API is already committed** (commit `e2f1707`). The relevant interfaces are
60: `GatekeeperUser.getVerifier()`, `GatekeeperUserVerifier`, `Gatekeeper.addObserver()` /
61: `removeObserver()`, and `ObservationDescription.excludeObservers`, all in
62: `packages/workshop-shared/src/gatekeeper.ts`.
63: 
64: ### v1 scope decisions (agreed)
65: 
66: - **No per-thread enforcement.** v1 is all-or-nothing per observer. We do not (yet) hide
67:   individual chat threads or observations from individual collaborators.
68: - **Role-based breadth of verification:**
69:   - **`build`** collaborators (full access — chat + code + all bindings) must be verified
70:     against **every** gatekeeper the Gadget has.
71:   - **`use`** collaborators (UI only, no chat access — see `UseOverseerInterface`,
72:     `overseer.ts:2816`) must be verified only against **named bindings** (gatekeepers with a
73:     `bindingName`), since that is all the UI can invoke.
74: - **Account selection.** A collaborator must have their own connected account for each vendor the
75:   Gadget depends on. For ordinary bindings, they choose which account to use (e.g. work or personal
76:   Google). If an account cannot be selected automatically, the configuration modal prompts them to
77:   choose or connect one; declining denies the open. Ambient bindings are the exception to account
78:   *selection*, not verification: when the collaborator already has the matching provided singleton
79:   account, the overseer uses it automatically and still runs the gatekeeper's normal `addObserver`
80:   check.
81: - **Authorization is keyed on the sharing table, not on live sessions.** Because a Gadget may
82:   *store* observed data and re-display it later (even to a `use` observer who opens much later),
83:   every exclusion/enforcement decision keys off whether a user is still *authorized* in the
84:   sharing graph (`computeEffectiveRoles`), never off whether they currently have the Gadget open.

108: ## 3. Concepts & terminology
109: 
110: - **Observer:** a non-owner collaborator (any role) who can see data the Gadget has read.
111: - **Sharing table:** the existing `collaborators` / `shareKeys` storage + permission graph
112:   (`sharing.ts`). Records the owner's **intent** that a user have access.
113: - **Observer record (new):** overseer storage describing a user who has **configured their
114:   gatekeeper accounts and passed all `addObserver` checks** — i.e. is actually set up to observe.
115:   This is distinct from the sharing table: intent vs. configured-and-verified. Opening requires
116:   **both** (reachable in the sharing graph AND a valid, complete observer record).
117: - **Observer ID:** a **random, opaque** string the overseer generates when it first creates an
118:   observer record, and stores in that record. It is passed to gatekeepers as the stable handle
119:   for this observer. We deliberately do **not** use `profile.id` (usually an email), to avoid
120:   tempting gatekeeper authors to parse identity out of it — identity is conveyed only via the
121:   verifier. The ID need not survive removal/re-add: a user who loses and regains access gets a
122:   fresh record and a fresh ID.
123: - **Verifier:** `Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier>` minted by the *observer's own*
124:   `GatekeeperUser` (a specific connected account they chose). A persistent service stub — no
125:   disposal required.
126: - **Invariant maintained:** for every user authorized in the sharing graph and every gatekeeper
127:   in scope for their role, the gatekeeper has confirmed (at the user's last open) that the user
128:   may observe everything read so far, AND no later observation has been allowed that the user may
129:   not see.

165: ## 5. Work breakdown
166: 
167: ### Step 1 — User DO: mint a verifier for a chosen account
168: 
169: Add a method to the User DO (`packages/workshop-backend/src/user.ts`), near
170: `getGatekeeperClassFor` (`user.ts:1136`):
171: 
172: ```ts
173: // Mint a verifier from one of THIS user's connected accounts, identified by accountId.
174: // Returns null if the account is missing. Throws if it belongs to a different vendor.
175: async getVerifier(
176:   accountId: number,
177:   expectedVendorId: string,
178: ): Promise<Fetcher<GatekeeperUserVerifier> | null>
179: ```
180: 
181: Implementation: look up `this.storage.connectedAccounts.get(accountId)` and compare its stored
182: vendor with `expectedVendorId` (exact match) before returning `account.account.getVerifier()`.
183: Account selection is done by the frontend, but this server-side check must not trust that filtering
184: (see Step 3). A missing account returns null (re-prompt); a vendor mismatch throws (not a
185: legitimate UI state).
186: 
187: > Promise pipelining: callers can pass the returned promise straight into `addObserver()` without
188: > awaiting it (see the Cap'n Web note in `AGENTS.md`). The observer-open path awaits it because a
189: > null result means the account must be re-selected before calling `addObserver()`.
190: 
191: ### Step 2 — Client-server API: a configuration callback on `open` / `openGadget`
192: 
193: We must avoid structured/typed errors for control flow (prohibited in this codebase) and must not
194: break promise pipelining in the common case. So `open()` gains an **optional callback** that is
195: invoked **only** when the opening user needs to configure gatekeeper accounts. In the common case
196: (owner, or an already-configured observer) the callback is never called, and `open()` resolves
197: without an extra round trip.
198: 
199: Add to the RPC API (`packages/workshop-shared/src/api.ts`) and thread through
200: `server.ts:206` → `overseer.open()` (`overseer.ts:2714`):
201: 
202: ```ts
203: // Provided by the client when opening a gadget. Invoked by the overseer only if the opening
204: // user must choose connected accounts for one or more gatekeeper bindings before they can
205: // observe the gadget. The overseer does not resolve open() until this returns.
206: interface ObserverConfigCallback extends RpcTarget {
207:   configure(needs: ObserverBindingNeed[]): Promise<ObserverAccountChoice[]>;
208: }
209: 
210: type ObserverBindingNeed = {
211:   gatekeeperId: number;
212:   vendorId: string;
213:   resourceTitle: string;
214:   resourceUrl?: string;
215: };
216: 
217: type ObserverAccountChoice = {
218:   gatekeeperId: number;
219:   accountId: number;   // an account in the opening user's own User DO
220: };
221: ```
222: 
223: `open()` signature gains `configureObservers?: RpcStub<ObserverConfigCallback>`.
224: 
225: (Same goes for `openGadget()`, which is the public-facing API method on `AuthenticatedApi`.)
226: 
227: ### Step 3 — Overseer: observer configuration & re-verification at `open()`
228: 
229: Hook into `open()` in the non-owner branch, after `effectiveRole` is confirmed and before
230: constructing the client interface. Keep the existing `prohibitAllSharing` short-circuit ahead of
231: this -- lockdown still wins. The `NeedsConnections` signal is produced only *after* a valid role is
232: confirmed, so it never reveals a workspace's gatekeeper or resource metadata to an unauthorized
233: user.
234: 
235: Add a private helper on `OverseerImpl`, roughly:
236: 
237: ```ts
238: // Bring `profileId` (a non-owner) into compliance as an observer for their `role`.
239: // May invoke `configureCb` to ask the user to choose accounts for not-yet-configured bindings.
240: // Re-verifies (re-runs addObserver) for already-configured bindings on every open.
241: // Returns when the user is fully verified; throws to deny access.
242: async ensureObserver(
243:     profileId: string,
244:     clientUser: Fetcher<User>,
245:     role: CollaboratorRole,
246:     configureCb?: RpcStub<ObserverConfigCallback>): Promise<void>
247: ```
248: 
249: Logic:
250: 
251: 1. **Select in-scope gatekeepers** from `this.storage.gatekeepers.list()`:
252:    - `build`: all gatekeepers.
253:    - `use`: only those with a `bindingName`.
254:    - A `creationSpec` with a `vendorId` requires an account; other specs need no verifier or account
255:      choice.
256: 
257: 2. **Load the observer record** for `profileId` (may be absent).
258: 
259: 3. **Determine uncovered bindings**: in-scope account-requiring gatekeepers with no
260:    `accountChoices` entry in the record. Before prompting, automatically fill ambient bindings from
261:    the collaborator's matching provided singleton accounts. Ordinary bindings, missing ambient
262:    accounts, and bindings being re-prompted after a failed verification remain uncovered.
263: 
264: 4. **If there are uncovered bindings**, invoke `configureCb.configure(needs)` with one
265:    `ObserverBindingNeed` per uncovered binding. If `configureCb` is absent (e.g. a non-interactive
266:    open), deny. Merge the returned `ObserverAccountChoice[]` into a working copy of the record's
267:    `accountChoices`.
268: 
269: 5. **Re-verify all in-scope bindings** (covered + newly chosen). For each, resolve the chosen
270:    account's verifier via `clientUser.getVerifier(accountId, bindingVendorId)` and call
271:    `this.getGatekeeperFacet(gk.id).addObserver(record.observerId, verifier)`. Generate
272:    `observerId` (random) if the record is new. Run these with `Promise.all` + pipelining where
273:    possible.
274:    - The User DO compares `bindingVendorId` with the chosen connected account's stored vendor and
275:      **throws** on a mismatch. This server-side check is what guarantees a gatekeeper only receives
276:      a verifier minted by its own vendor; filtering account choices in the client is only a
277:      user-interface convenience.
278:    - If any `addObserver` **throws** (or `getVerifier` throws on vendor mismatch), the user is not
279:      (or no longer) allowed: best-effort `removeObserver(record.observerId)` on the gatekeepers
280:      added in *this* pass, do **not** persist the working record, and deny the open with a clear
281:      message.
282: 
283: 6. **Persist the observer record** (with merged `accountChoices` and `observerId`) only after all
284:    `addObserver` calls succeed. Storing/creating the record is the canonical moment the user
285:    becomes a configured observer; its later deletion is what triggers `removeObserver` (Steps 5
286:    and 6).
287: 
288: Then in `open()`:
289: 
290: ```ts
291: await this.impl.ensureObserver(profileId, clientUser, role, configureObservers);
292: ```
293: 
294: Notes:
295: - **Re-verification every open is intentional.** It catches revocation of the user's underlying
296:   resource access promptly (caught at their next open). Gatekeepers for which re-running
297:   `addObserver` on every open is expensive should implement their own caching strategy — it is up
298:   to each gatekeeper to choose the right tradeoff between performance and immediacy of revocation.
299: - Re-verification of already-covered bindings does **not** pop the modal; it silently reuses the
300:   stored account choices. The modal is only for genuinely uncovered bindings (first open, a binding
301:   the owner added after this user last configured, or an ambient binding without a matching provided
302:   account).

304: ### Step 4 — Frontend: the configuration modal
305: 
306: Implement the `ObserverConfigCallback` on the client. When the overseer calls `configure(needs)`:
307: 
308: 1. For each `ObserverBindingNeed`, find the user's candidate accounts by filtering the existing
309:    `subscribeConnectedAccounts()` results (`user.ts:890`) by `need.vendorId`.
310: 2. If one or more accounts match, pre-select one arbitrarily as the default; let the user change
311:    it via a dropdown. (Most users have one account per vendor and will just click "OK".)
312: 3. Include forced auto-provisioned accounts in the subscription. If **no** account matches, use
313:    `listAddableGatekeepers()` to identify optional auto-provisioning vendors and provision those
314:    directly; otherwise use the existing `connectAccount` flow. Then include the new account as the
315:    choice.
316: 4. Resolve `configure()` with one `ObserverAccountChoice` per binding. If the user cancels / can't
317:    provide an account, reject (the overseer denies the open and the UI shows an access-denied
318:    state).
319: 
320: Messaging: "To open this Gadget, choose which of your «Vendor» accounts to use, so we can confirm
321: you're allowed to see the data it uses."
322: 
323: ### Step 5 — Overseer: forward exclusion in `authorizeObservation()`
324: 
325: Extend `authorizeObservation()` (`overseer.ts:1169`) to honor `description.excludeObservers`.
326: Because v1 has no per-thread hiding, the only case in which we can let an excluded-but-named
327: observation proceed is when the named observer has *already lost access* in the sharing graph.
328: 
329: For each id in `description.excludeObservers`:
330: 
331: 1. Map the opaque `observerId` → `profileId` via the `observers.byObserverId` index. If there is
332:    no record, the id is not an active observer → ignore it.
333: 2. Check sharing-graph reachability for that `profileId`
334:    (`SharingManager.getEffectiveRole` / `computeEffectiveRoles`).
335:    - **Still authorized → throw**, blocking the observation (degrade to per-observation
336:      lockdown). Use a clear message, e.g.:
337:      `"This observation was blocked because it contains data that a current collaborator is not permitted to see."`
338:    - **No longer authorized → allow** for this observer, and **delete their observer record**
339:      (and best-effort `removeObserver(observerId)` on all gatekeepers). They are no longer set up
340:      to observe; if they ever regain access they reconfigure from scratch (Step 3).
341: 3. If, after evaluating all excluded ids, none are still-authorized, allow the observation.
342: 
343: This is the runtime counterpart of `addObserver`: `addObserver` covers observers configured
344: *after* data was read; `excludeObservers` covers data read *after* observers were configured.
345: Persisting the observation record itself is unchanged; we only gate it.
346: 
347: > Why not also worry about authorized-but-not-yet-configured users here? They cannot be named in
348: > `excludeObservers` because no gatekeeper knows their id yet. The invariant still holds from the
349: > other direction: when such a user later opens and configures, `addObserver` re-checks them
350: > against *all* past observations (including any restricted one) and throws, denying them. So
351: > forward exclusion only needs to handle already-configured observers.
352: 
353: ### Step 6 — Overseer: remove observers on sharing changes
354: 
355: When sharing changes, configured observers who lose access must be torn down. In the overseer
356: methods wrapping `SharingManager` mutations (`removeCollaborator`, `revokeShareLink`, and role
357: downgrades — see the matching methods on `OverseerClientInterface` and `SharingManager`):
358: 
359: - After a mutation, use the returned `AffectedCollaborator[]` to find users who **lost access**.
360:   For each who is now unreachable, if they have an observer record: best-effort
361:   `removeObserver(record.observerId)` on **all** gatekeeper facets, then delete the observer
362:   record.
363: - For a **`build` → `use` downgrade**, optionally `removeObserver` (and drop the corresponding
364:   `accountChoices` entries) for the now-out-of-scope bindings (those without a `bindingName`).
365:   Safe to defer — an over-broad observer set only ever errs toward stricter future checks — but
366:   it keeps gatekeeper state tidy.
367: - All these calls are best-effort: log and continue on error. An orphaned observer entry only
368:   causes superfluous future checks, never a data leak (the leak-relevant gate is
369:   `authorizeObservation`, which keys off the live sharing graph).
370: 
371: > Multi-gatekeeper sequencing/atomicity is an overseer implementation detail, not part of the
372: > shared interface. Because `addObserver` is re-run every open and `removeObserver` is idempotent,
373: > a failure mid-teardown self-heals: the next open re-verifies, and `authorizeObservation`'s
374: > sharing-graph check is always authoritative regardless of stale gatekeeper memory.
375: 
376: ### Step 7 — Gatekeeper interface contract (hand-off note)
377: 
378: The per-gatekeeper implementations are out of scope (separate plans), but to keep the Workshop
379: and gatekeeper teams aligned, document the contract the Workshop relies on. Most of this is
380: already in the JSDoc in `gatekeeper.ts`; add anything missing there rather than duplicating:
381: 
382: - `getVerifier()` returns a persistent service stub representing the calling user's account; the
383:   Workshop only ever passes it back to the *same vendor* that minted it.
384: - `addObserver(observerId, verifier)` MUST throw if the user represented by `verifier` is not
385:   allowed to observe everything read through this gatekeeper so far. The Workshop calls it on
386:   every open of every authorized observer (re-verification); gatekeepers should cache as needed.
387: - `removeObserver(observerId)` MUST be idempotent.
388: - A gatekeeper that wants to restrict a future observation to a subset of observers sets
389:   `excludeObservers` (the opaque ids it was given) on the `ObservationDescription`; the Workshop
390:   will block the observation unless every named observer has already lost access.

394: ## 6. Edge cases
395: 
396: 1. **Owner is never an observer** — the owner always has `build` and is excluded from the
397:    collaborators table; `ensureObserver` runs for non-owners only.
398: 2. **Collaborator disconnects a chosen account later** — next open,
399:    `getVerifier(accountId, bindingVendorId)` returns null; treat the affected binding as uncovered
400:    and re-prompt via the modal. A mismatched-vendor account (only reachable by bypassing the UI)
401:    throws and denies the open.
402: 3. **Underlying resource access revoked** — caught at the next open because `addObserver`
403:    re-runs the live check and throws; the open is denied. Consistent with the lazy-revocation
404:    model in `sharing.ts`.
405: 4. **`prohibitAllSharing` interaction** — unchanged and still authoritative: if set, no non-owner
406:    can open at all (`overseer.ts:2770`). Observer checks only matter when sharing is allowed.
407: 5. **Owner adds a new binding after sharing** — existing observers see an incremental modal for
408:    just the new binding on their next open, and may be denied if they lack access to the new
409:    resource (inherent to the security model).
410: 6. **Performance** — `ensureObserver` does one `getVerifier` + one `addObserver` per in-scope
411:    gatekeeper per open. Parallelize with `Promise.all` and pipe the verifier promise straight into
412:    `addObserver`. Expensive gatekeepers cache on their side.
413: 7. **`use`-role observers and `excludeObservers`** — `use` observers are only configured against
414:    named bindings, so they will never appear in `excludeObservers` from a non-named binding (the
415:    gatekeeper doesn't know their id). The Step 5 logic handles this naturally (unknown id →
416:    ignored).

463: ## 9. Per-gatekeeper observer-tracking strategy
464: 
465: This section records the **strategy decision** for each existing gatekeeper — i.e. *how* each one
466: should satisfy the `addObserver` / `removeObserver` / `getVerifier` contract from §7. The actual
467: implementation of each is still a separate follow-up plan (sequencing step 6 above); this section
468: fixes the approach so those plans can proceed consistently.
469: 
470: ### 9.1 Strategies
471: 
472: Strategy is chosen **per resource type** (per `Gatekeeper` DO class / binding), **not** per
473: gatekeeper package — a single package (e.g. `gatekeeper-google`) may use several strategies across
474: its resource types.
475: 
476: - **A — Private-only.** Non-owner observers are refused: `addObserver()` unconditionally throws.
477:   This is the replacement for today's reliance on `prohibitAllSharing` for these resources (the
478:   `prohibitAllSharing` lockdown mechanism itself is unchanged and remains available separately).
479:   `getVerifier()` must still exist (the overseer mints one on every open) but is never consulted.
480: 
481: - **B — ACL check (single unit).** The resource is treated as one atomic unit.
482:   `getVerifier()` mints a verifier exposing the observer's vendor identity (via the
483:   "non-standard method on the verifier" pattern, `gatekeeper.ts:456-461`). `addObserver()` resolves
484:   that identity and checks it against the bound resource's ACL, throwing on failure. Gatekeepers
485:   should cache per-open to bound cost (`gatekeeper.ts:511-516`). No `excludeObservers` is needed:
486:   the whole unit is covered up front, so nothing read later could be invisible to a verified
487:   observer.
488: 
489: - **C — Data-set tracking.** The `Gatekeeper` DO maintains its own log of the **data sets** it has
490:   actually observed (e.g. BigQuery dataset, Linear team, Notion page/database, Supabase project),
491:   plus the set of current observers. `addObserver()` verifies the observer against **every** logged
492:   set so far. When a later observation first touches a **new** set, the gatekeeper re-verifies all
493:   current observers and sets `excludeObservers` for any who fail (the overseer then blocks the
494:   observation per `gatekeeper.ts:751-774`). `removeObserver()` drops the observer from the tracked
495:   set. Each per-set check reuses the same ACL primitive the corresponding narrow (B) binding uses.
496: 
497: - **D — Low-stakes.** No information-flow tracking. `addObserver()` / `removeObserver()` are
498:   no-ops; any collaborator may observe. `getVerifier()` returns a trivial verifier (the overseer
499:   still calls it, so it must exist and not throw).
500: 
501: - **N — N/A.** The gatekeeper exposes no resources, so it is never an in-scope binding; nothing to
502:   implement.
503: 
504: ### 9.2 Decision table
505: 
506: | Gatekeeper | Resource type / binding | Strategy | `addObserver` behavior |
507: |---|---|---|---|
508: | **cloudflare** | (no resources — auth only) | **N** | Never in scope; nothing to implement. |
509: | **email** | Email Mailbox | **D** | No-op. Synthetic per-gadget inbound address; the gadget's collaborators are the intended audience. |
510: | **spotify** | Account / Playlist | **D** | No-op. Personal, low-stakes; no corp-security concern. |
511: | **homeassistant** | Instance / Area / Label / Device / Entity | **D** | No-op. Self-hosted personal; the pasted long-lived token is all-or-nothing and HA exposes no per-user/per-entity ACL oracle to check against. |
512: | **github** | Repo / Issue / PR | **B** | Check the observer's GitHub identity has read access to the bound repo (public → always pass; private → collaborator/org-team check). Issues/PRs inherit the repo ACL, so the repo is the atomic unit. |
513: | **google** | Google Doc | **B** | Check the observer's Drive sharing access to the bound document. |
514: | **google** | Google Spreadsheet | **B** | Check the observer's Google Sheets access to the bound spreadsheet. Spreadsheet sharing applies to the whole file, so it is the atomic unit. |
515: | **google** | Google Calendar (selected calendar) | **B** | Require `writer` or `owner` access to the bound calendar, since `reader` access hides private-event details. Future: let the binding owner exclude private events so readers can collaborate. |
516: | **google** | Google Calendar (`allVisible` availability) | **C** | In addition to the selected-calendar check, track foreign calendars whose free/busy data was successfully read and verify each observer can independently query their availability. |
517: | **google** | Gmail Mailbox | **A** | Always throw. (Future: allow observers who independently have access, e.g. mailing-list members — explicitly out of scope now.) |
518: | **google** | BigQuery | **C** | Track accessed datasets; verify the observer's IAM access to each. Dataset granularity for now (tables/columns later). |
519: | **linear** | Team / Issue | **B** | Check the observer's workspace/team membership, honoring team privacy. |
520: | **linear** | Workspace | **C** | Track accessed teams; verify the observer against each (reusing the Team B check). |
521: | **notion** | Page / Database | **B** | Check the observer's Notion access to the bound page/database. |
522: | **notion** | Workspace | **C** | Track accessed pages/databases; verify the observer's access to each. |
523: | **supabase** | Project | **B** | Verify the observer's own `listProjects()` (`supabase-api.ts:306`) includes the bound project ref. Within a project, arbitrary read-only SQL spans the whole DB, so the project is the atomic unit (no per-table tracking). |
524: | **supabase** | Organization | **C** | Track accessed project refs (the org session reaches them via `openProject` / `listProjects`, `supabase.ts:1015`/`:1037`); verify the observer's `listProjects()` includes each, reusing the Project B check. |
525: | **confluence** | Site | **C** | Verify site access; track observed spaces and content because both can have narrower permissions. |
526: | **confluence** | Space | **C** | Verify space access; track observed pages and blog posts because content restrictions may be narrower. |
527: | **confluence** | Page / Blog Post | **C** | Verify bound-content access; track observed child pages because they may have stricter restrictions than their parent. |
528: | **zoominfo** | Account | **A** | Always throw. The whole-account binding exposes licensed, entitlement-dependent and account-specific intelligence, and ZoomInfo provides no ACL oracle proving another account can read every historical result. |
529: | **context** | Context Library singleton | **C** | Track observed collections; verify each is public in the sharing domain or privately owned by the observer's Context account. |
530: 
531: ### 9.3 The "broad binding" lens
532: 
533: Several packages expose both a broad binding and narrower ones. A broad binding should use **C**
534: (track the sub-resources actually touched, verifying each with the narrow binding's ACL primitive)
535: only when **both** of these hold:
536: 
537: 1. The broad binding spans sub-resources that have **distinct ACLs** (otherwise one ACL already
538:    covers everything — use B).
539: 2. There is a **per-observer access oracle** to check each sub-resource against (otherwise you can
540:    log what was touched but cannot verify anyone against it).
541: 
542: This is why the broad bindings split the way they do:
543: 
544: - **Satisfy both → C:** Supabase Org (projects + `listProjects()` oracle), Linear Workspace
545:   (teams + membership), Notion Workspace (pages + page access), BigQuery (datasets + IAM), Context
546:   Library (public/private collections + account/domain ownership checks).
547: - **Fail criterion 1 → B:** GitHub Repository — issues/PRs/discussions/code all inherit the single
548:   repo permission, and there is no binding broader than one repo, so the repo is the atomic ACL
549:   unit.
550: - **Fail criterion 2 → D (or A):** Home Assistant Instance — areas/devices/entities exist but the
551:   long-lived token is all-or-nothing and HA has no per-user ACL oracle, so there is nothing to
552:   verify an observer against. (Spotify is moot: ACL enforcement is off entirely under D.)
553: - **Decomposition deliberately deferred → A:** Gmail Mailbox — could in principle decompose into
554:   mailing lists the observer belongs to, but that is the out-of-scope "advanced" case, so it stays
555:   fully private for now.

(End of file - total 555 lines)
</content>
